questions.question: What is Git and why is it called a distributed version control system?
questions.title: What Is Git?
questions.direct_answer: Git is a distributed version control system where every developer has a full copy of the entire project history on their local machine, unlike centralized systems that rely on a single server. This means you can commit, branch, and view history without network access.

sections.title: Git as a Distributed Version Control System
sections.content: **Git** is a version control system (VCS) that tracks changes to files over time, letting you recall specific versions, see who changed what, and collaborate with others. The key word is **distributed**: unlike older systems where only a central server holds the full history, every developer who clones a Git repository gets the entire project history on their machine. Think of it like everyone having a complete backup of a shared library, not just borrowing books from one location. This architecture makes Git fast — commits, diffs, and history browsing happen locally without network latency. It also makes Git resilient: if the central server crashes, any developer's clone can restore the entire project. The distributed model unlocks offline work, fast branching, and decentralized collaboration workflows that centralized systems simply can't support.

sections.title: Creating and Working with a Git Repository
Key Points
content: **Distributed**: Every developer has the full repository history locally, not just the latest files
**Local operations**: Commits, branches, merges, and history viewing happen on your machine without network calls
**Offline capability**: You can commit and view history on a plane or without VPN access to the central server
**.git directory**: Git stores all history and metadata in a single hidden folder at the repository root
**Speed**: Local operations are orders of magnitude faster than contacting a remote server for every action
**Resilience**: Any clone can restore the full project if the central server is lost
**Git vs GitHub**: Git is the version control tool; GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket are hosting services for Git repos

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Git is a distributed version control system, which means every developer gets a full copy of the entire project history on their local machine. It's not just the current files — you get every commit, every branch, everything. This is different from older centralized systems where only the server has the complete history. The distributed design gives you two huge advantages. First, speed. Since the history is local, operations like committing or viewing logs are instant — no network round trip. Second, offline capability. You can commit changes, create branches, and explore history on a flight or when the VPN is down. A common mistake freshers make is thinking Git and GitHub are the same thing. They're not. Git is the version control tool itself. GitHub is just a hosting service where teams store their Git repositories online. You could use GitLab or Bitbucket instead, and Git would work exactly the same way. The distributed architecture also makes Git resilient. If your company's GitHub server crashes, any developer's local clone can restore the entire project. That's why distributed version control became the industry standard for modern software development.

questions.title: Git vs SVN

sections.title: Git vs SVN: Distributed vs Centralized Models
sections.content: **Git** and **SVN** (Subversion) are both version control systems, but they use fundamentally different architectures. SVN is **centralized**: there's one master repository on a server, and developers check out working copies. Every commit, update, and history query goes to that central server. Git is **distributed**: every developer clones the full repository, including all history, and works locally. Commits happen on your machine first, then you push to a shared remote. This architectural difference cascades into workflow differences. Git enables fast branching and merging because branches are local pointers. SVN branching is slow because it involves copying directories on the server. Git lets you commit offline. SVN requires network access for commits. Both solve the same problem — tracking changes — but Git's distributed model is better suited to modern distributed teams and continuous integration pipelines.

sections.title: When to Choose Git vs SVN
sections.content: Use **Git** when you need distributed workflows, fast branching, or offline capability. Most modern software teams use Git because it fits continuous integration and feature-branch workflows. Remote teams benefit from local commits and the ability to work without VPN. Git's branching model makes it easy to experiment and merge changes. Use **SVN** when you need fine-grained access control over specific files or directories. Some enterprises with strict compliance requirements prefer SVN because they can control who accesses each part of the codebase at the server level. SVN also has a simpler mental model for teams unfamiliar with distributed concepts, though this is less relevant as Git has become the industry default. In practice, Git dominates modern development, but understanding why SVN still exists shows you appreciate the trade-offs.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Distributed vs centralized**: Git gives every developer the full history; SVN keeps history only on the server
**Commit model**: Git commits locally then pushes; SVN commits directly to the central repository
**Branching performance**: Git branches are lightweight pointers; SVN branches copy entire directory structures
**Offline work**: Git lets you commit and branch without network; SVN requires server access for most operations
**Access control granularity**: SVN allows per-file permissions; Git controls access at the repository level
**Industry adoption**: Git is the default for modern projects; SVN persists in legacy enterprise environments
**Learning curve**: Git's distributed model is conceptually harder but more powerful for team workflows

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The main difference is that Git is distributed and SVN is centralized. In SVN, there's one central server that holds the entire history. Developers check out a working copy, and when they commit, it goes straight to that server. If the server's down or you don't have network access, you can't commit. Git is distributed, so when you clone a repository, you get the full history locally. You commit to your local repository first, then push those commits to a shared remote. This means you can commit changes on a plane or when the VPN is down. Another big difference is branching. In Git, creating a branch is instant — it's just a pointer to a commit. In SVN, branching copies the entire directory tree on the server, which is slow and heavyweight. That's why Git workflows rely heavily on feature branches, but SVN projects often avoid branching. A fresher mistake is saying Git is always better. It's not that simple. SVN has fine-grained access control — you can restrict who sees specific files or folders. Some enterprises with strict security policies still use SVN for that reason. But for most modern teams, Git's distributed model is the right fit. It's faster, supports offline work, and integrates better with continuous integration pipelines.

questions.question: What are the three areas (or stages) in Git's local workflow?
questions.title: Git's Three Areas: Working Directory, Staging Area, Repository
questions.direct_answer: Git has three areas: the working directory (where you edit files), the staging area or index (where you prepare the next commit), and the local repository (the committed history stored in .git). This three-stage model gives you fine control over what goes into each commit.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Git's internal model — this is foundational for understanding add/commit/stash
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking 'commit' goes directly from the working directory — the staging step is often missed
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why the staging area is useful — you can commit only a subset of your changes

sections.title: Git's Three-Stage Workflow Model
sections.content: Git organizes your work into three distinct areas: the **working directory**, the **staging area** (also called the index), and the **local repository**. The **working directory** is where you edit files — your actual project folder. The **staging area** is an intermediate zone where you prepare changes for the next commit. The **local repository** is the committed history stored in the hidden .git directory. This three-stage model is unique to Git and gives you precise control. You might change five files but only want to commit three — stage those three with git add, then commit. The staging area acts like a shopping cart: you add items you want, review them with git status, and finalize the purchase with git commit. This design might feel like extra steps at first, but it enables powerful workflows like committing logical chunks of work separately even if they're mixed in the same files.

sections.title: Moving Changes Through Git's Three Areas
Key Points
content: **Working directory**: The actual project files you edit — untracked or modified files live here
**Staging area (index)**: A preparation zone where you build the next commit using git add
**Local repository**: The committed history stored in the .git directory — permanent snapshots
**git add**: Moves changes from working directory to staging area — you're choosing what to commit
**git commit**: Moves staged changes from staging area to local repository — finalizes the snapshot
**Selective staging**: You can stage only specific files or even specific lines, enabling fine-grained commits
**git status**: Shows which area your changes are in — unstaged in working dir or staged in index

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Git has three areas in its local workflow. First, the working directory — that's just your project folder where you edit files. Second, the staging area, also called the index. This is where you prepare the next commit. Third, the local repository, which is the committed history stored in the hidden dot-git directory. The flow goes like this. You edit a file in the working directory. Then you run git add to move those changes to the staging area. Finally, you run git commit to move the staged changes into the local repository as a permanent snapshot. A common mistake freshers make is thinking git commit takes changes directly from the working directory. It doesn't. It only commits what's in the staging area. That's why if you modify a file after staging it, you need to run git add again to stage the new changes. The staging area might seem like an extra step, but it's actually really useful. Let's say you changed five files but only three are related to the bug fix you're committing. You can stage just those three with git add and commit them together. The other two stay in the working directory for a separate commit later. This gives you precise control over commit granularity. Understanding these three areas is foundational because commands like git reset, git checkout, and git stash all manipulate which area your changes are in.

questions.question: Is a Git commit a diff (set of changes) or a snapshot of the entire project?
questions.title: Git Commits Are Snapshots, Not Diffs
questions.direct_answer: A Git commit is a snapshot of all tracked files at that point in time, not a diff — though Git is smart about storing only changed content to save space. Each commit points to a complete tree of file contents, not just the delta from the previous commit.

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of understanding of Git internals — separates candidates who've truly learned Git from those who've just used it

sections.title: Git Commits Store Snapshots, Not Diffs
sections.content: A **Git commit** is a full snapshot of your project at a point in time, not a set of changes (diff) from the previous commit. Each commit points to a **tree object** that represents the complete directory structure and file contents. This is conceptually different from systems like SVN, which store deltas (changesets). Think of Git commits like photographs taken every few minutes: each photo shows the entire scene, not just what changed since the last photo. However, Git isn't wasteful — it uses **content-addressable storage** with SHA-1 hashes. If a file hasn't changed between commits, Git stores only one copy of that file's content (a **blob object**) and both commits point to the same blob. This snapshot model makes operations like checkout, branch switching, and history traversal very fast because Git doesn't have to reconstruct file states by replaying deltas. You just point to the commit and you have the full state.

sections.title: Visualizing Git's Snapshot Model
Key Points
content: **Snapshot model**: Each commit stores a full tree of file contents, not just changes from the previous commit
**Tree object**: A commit points to a tree that represents the complete directory structure at that moment
**Blob objects**: File contents are stored as blobs identified by SHA-1 hash of the content
**Deduplication**: If a file is unchanged, multiple commits reuse the same blob — storage is efficient
**Fast operations**: Checkout and branch switching are fast because Git doesn't replay deltas to reconstruct state
**Content-addressable**: Git identifies objects by content hash, not name — two identical files share one blob
**Contrast with SVN**: SVN stores deltas (changesets); Git stores snapshots but optimizes storage with deduplication

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A Git commit is a snapshot of all tracked files at that point in time, not a diff. This surprises people because systems like SVN store commits as changesets — just the lines that were added or removed. Git doesn't work that way. Each commit points to a tree object that represents the entire project structure and file contents at that moment. It's like taking a photograph of your project every time you commit. Now, you might think that's wasteful — if you have a thousand commits, are you storing a thousand copies of every file? No. Git is smart about storage. It uses content-addressable storage with SHA-1 hashes. When you commit, Git creates blob objects for each file's content. The blob is identified by the hash of the content. If a file doesn't change between commits, both commits point to the same blob. Only one copy is stored. This snapshot model makes Git really fast. When you check out a commit or switch branches, Git doesn't have to replay a series of diffs to reconstruct the file state. It just points to the snapshot and you have the full state immediately. A common mistake is saying Git commits store diffs. They don't. Diffs are computed on demand when you run commands like git diff or git log, but they're not how commits are stored. This snapshot architecture is one reason Git outperforms older version control systems.

questions.question: What is the difference between git init and git clone?
questions.title: git init vs git clone
questions.direct_answer: git init creates a brand new empty repository in the current folder; git clone copies an existing remote repository (including all history) to your local machine. Use init when starting a new project from scratch, clone when joining an existing project.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic Git command knowledge and when to use each
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using git init on a project that already exists on GitHub instead of git clone
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that git clone also sets up the 'origin' remote automatically and configures tracking branches

sections.title: Starting a Repository: git init vs git clone
sections.content: **git init** and **git clone** are two ways to start working with a Git repository, but they serve different scenarios. **git init** creates a brand new repository in the current directory. It initializes an empty .git folder with no commits, no remotes, no history. You use it when you're starting a project from scratch on your machine. **git clone**, on the other hand, copies an existing repository from a remote location (like GitHub) to your local machine. It downloads the entire commit history, all branches, and automatically sets up a remote connection called origin pointing back to the source. Clone is what you use when joining an existing project. The key difference: init starts fresh with zero history, clone brings down an existing repository's complete state.

sections.title: When to Use git init vs git clone
sections.content: Use **git init** when you're starting a completely new project on your machine. For example, you create a new folder for a Java Spring Boot app, write some code, and want to start tracking it with Git. Run git init, then make your first commit. Later, if you want to push to GitHub, you manually add a remote with git remote add origin and push. Use **git clone** when a project already exists on a remote server and you want to work on it. Your team has a Java microservice on GitHub, and you need a local copy. Run git clone with the repository URL. Clone downloads everything — all commits, all branches, the entire history — and sets up origin to point back to GitHub. It also configures tracking branches so your local main tracks origin/main. A common fresher mistake is using git init on a folder and then trying to manually recreate a project that already exists remotely. Just use git clone instead. It's faster and sets up all the remote connections automatically.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **git init**: Creates a new empty Git repository in the current directory with no commits or remotes
**git clone <url>**: Copies an existing remote repository to your local machine with full history
**origin remote**: git clone automatically sets up a remote named origin pointing to the source URL
**Tracking branches**: Clone configures local branches to track corresponding remote branches for easy push/pull
**Use init for**: Starting a brand new project that doesn't exist anywhere else yet
**Use clone for**: Joining an existing project hosted on GitHub, GitLab, or a team server
**Common mistake**: Running git init when you should clone — this loses the connection to the remote and requires manual setup

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: git init and git clone both start a Git repository, but they're used in different situations. git init creates a brand new empty repository in your current folder. It sets up the dot-git directory with no commits, no branches, no remotes. You'd use it when you're starting a project from scratch. For example, you create a new Java project, write some code, and decide to version control it. You run git init, then make your first commit. git clone is different. It copies an existing repository from a remote location like GitHub to your local machine. When you clone, you get the entire commit history, all the branches, everything. It also sets up a remote connection called origin that points back to the source URL. You use clone when you're joining an existing project. Your team has a Spring Boot app on GitHub, and you need a local copy to start contributing. You run git clone with the URL, and you're ready to go. A big advantage of clone is that it automatically configures tracking branches. Your local main branch will track origin/main, so git pull and git push know where to sync with. If you use git init, you have to set up those remote connections manually with git remote add. A common mistake is using git init on a project that already exists on GitHub. Don't do that. Use git clone instead. It's faster, and it sets up all the remote plumbing for you automatically.
